subject: Vocabulary
topic: Idioms and Expressions — Meanings and Usage (W11 B2)

questions.stem: What does 'TURN OVER A NEW LEAF' mean?

options.option_text: To start reading a new book
To change one's behaviour for the better
To discover a new path in life
To abandon all previous work

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Turn over a new leaf' = to make a fresh start; to change one's behaviour or attitude for the better. Example: 'After the bad grades, he decided to turn over a new leaf and study harder.' Origin: 'leaf' here means a PAGE of a book (archaic) — turning to a new, blank page = starting fresh. Trap: 'Start reading a new book' = the literal reading; the idiom is entirely figurative.

options.option_text: To injure someone physically
To ask someone for help
To tease or joke with someone
To deceive someone with malicious intent

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Pull someone's leg' = to tease, joke, or trick someone in a playful and lighthearted way (without malicious intent). Example: 'Don't worry, I'm just pulling your leg — your presentation was great!' Trap: 'Deceive with malicious intent' = this is close but the idiom is specifically PLAYFUL (not harmful deception). 'Physically injure' = literal reading (wrong).

questions.stem: What does 'BITE OFF MORE THAN YOU CAN CHEW' mean?

options.option_text: To eat too much food at one sitting
To take on more responsibility than one can handle
To be greedy about food or possessions
To fail to complete a simple task

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Bite off more than you can chew' = to attempt or take on a task that is too large or difficult to handle. Example: 'By accepting five projects simultaneously, she bit off more than she could chew.' Trap: 'Eat too much' = the literal interpretation (wrong — it's about over-commitment, not overeating); 'Greedy' = partially related but doesn't capture the 'inability to complete' aspect.

questions.stem: What does 'HAVE AN AXE TO GRIND' mean?

options.option_text: To look for a sharpening tool
To have a personal reason for doing something; a selfish motive
To want to resolve a conflict quickly
To work hard with simple tools

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Have an axe to grind' = to have a hidden personal motive or grievance behind one's actions; an ulterior motive. Example: 'He always seems to have an axe to grind when he criticises the government — he was sacked by them once.' The idiom implies the person is not acting from pure principle but from personal interest or resentment. Trap: 'Resolve a conflict quickly' = unrelated; the idiom implies unresolved personal grievance, not resolution.

questions.stem: What does 'KEEP THE BALL ROLLING' mean?

options.option_text: To maintain a game of ball sports
To keep moving around
To ensure an activity continues without interruption
To start a new project from scratch

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Keep the ball rolling' = to maintain progress or momentum; to ensure that an activity or discussion continues. Example: 'She kept the conversation rolling with interesting questions.' Contrast with 'GET the ball rolling' (= start an activity) vs 'KEEP the ball rolling' (= continue it). Trap: 'Start a new project' = 'GET the ball rolling' (different idiom); 'Keep moving around' = literal reading.

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of 'BURN THE BRIDGES' in: 'By resigning publicly, he burned his bridges with the firm.'

options.option_text: Created new opportunities
Damaged relationships permanently, making return impossible
Built a strong reputation
Left the company on good terms

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Burn one's bridges' = to take an irreversible action that prevents any possibility of return or reconciliation; to permanently sever a relationship or connection. Origin: military — burning bridges behind you in retreat prevents you from going back. Example: Resigning publicly in an embarrassing way = burning bridges (can't return). Trap: 'Left on good terms' = opposite meaning; 'New opportunities' = could follow bridge-burning but is not what the idiom means.

questions.stem: What does 'BLOW ONE'S OWN TRUMPET' mean?

options.option_text: To play a musical instrument
To boast about one's own achievements
To lead a parade
To announce something to the public

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Blow one's own trumpet' (British English) = 'Blow one's own horn' (American English) = to boast or brag about one's own achievements or abilities. Example: 'He never misses an opportunity to blow his own trumpet about his academic results.' Trap: 'Announce something to the public' = somewhat related but not the idiomatic meaning (which specifically = self-promotion/boasting).

questions.stem: What does 'MAKE BOTH ENDS MEET' mean?

options.option_text: To complete a project successfully
To join two groups together
To earn just enough money to cover basic expenses
To travel from one place to another

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Make both ends meet' (or 'make ends meet') = to manage to live within one's income; to earn just enough to cover one's expenses without going into debt. Example: 'With two jobs, she barely makes ends meet.' Origin: 'ends' refers to income (one end) and expenditure (other end) — making them 'meet' = balancing the budget. Trap: 'Complete a project' = unrelated; 'Join two groups' = literal misreading.

questions.stem: What does 'HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD' mean?

options.option_text: To injure someone accidentally
To succeed in hitting a target in carpentry
To describe exactly what is true or correct
To identify the most important person in a group

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Hit the nail on the head' = to describe exactly or identify precisely what the problem, cause, or issue is. Example: 'You've hit the nail on the head — the real problem is lack of communication.' Trap: 'Succeed in carpentry' = the literal meaning (not the figurative idiom); 'Identify the most important person' = unrelated (the idiom is about being precisely correct, not about identifying people).

options.option_text: To weep loudly in public
To give a false alarm; to raise unnecessary panic
To ask for help when in genuine danger
To warn others about a dangerous animal

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Cry wolf' = to raise a false alarm; to call for help when none is needed, so that when real help is needed, no one believes you. Origin: Aesop's fable of the boy who cried wolf (falsely) until no one came when a real wolf appeared. Example: 'He cried wolf so often about deadlines that no one took his latest warning seriously.' Trap: 'Warn about a dangerous animal' = the literal content of the fable (not the idiomatic meaning); 'Ask for genuine help' = the OPPOSITE of what the idiom means.
